raw_case_text:
A 5-year-old previously healthy male was referred to our institution for further evaluation of a liver mass. By history, he developed fatigue after participation in a fishing tournament 4 weeks prior to presentation followed by abdominal pain the next day. He was taken to the local hospital for evaluation of his symptoms where he was found to have a fever of 38.9 C. His evaluation included routine laboratory testing and chest X-ray. Based on chest X-ray findings and his symptoms, he was diagnosed with pneumonia and was treated with antibiotics. His abdominal pain at that time was thought to be referred pain. He completed a course of antibiotics but continued to have mild abdominal pain. A CT scan of the abdomen was done for further evaluation of his persistent abdominal pain, and it showed a multicystic-appearing lesion within the inferior aspect of the right hepatic lobe. Subsequently, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) exam of the abdomen was performed to further evaluate the hepatic mass. The MRI showed multiple serpiginous tubular-type structures predominantly within segment 5 with questionable peripherally located foci of T2 signal hyperintensity seen within the structures. These findings were thought to be consistent with possible focal Caroli syndrome. At that time, laboratory evaluation showed normal liver function tests with a prothrombin time (PT) of 11.6 sec; international normalization ratio (INR) 1.1; fibrinogen 435 mg/dL; alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 21 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 26 U/L; and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) 10 U/L. His inflammatory markers were slightly elevated with CRP 5.4 and ESR 30. His alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) was normal (0.8 IU/mL). Antibodies to Entamoeba histolytica and Echinococcus were checked and were negative. Because of persistent abdominal pain and no clear diagnosis of his liver mass, the patient was then referred to our institution.
The review of the MRI at our institution showed clusters of multiple T2-bright circumscribed cystic lesions in segment 6 measuring <2 cm in greatest dimension which was suggestive of mesenchymal hamartoma (Figure 1). Pediatric surgery was consulted, and he subsequently underwent a hepatic lobectomy with resection of the ~6 x 12 cm mass (Figure 2). The pathological review of the resected mass showed puzzle-shaped pieces of hepatic parenchyma embedded in hyalinized matrix (hematoxylin and eosin stain with 200x magnification), consistent with a mesenchymal hamartoma (Figure 3). The patient did well postoperatively and was asymptomatic at the time of his follow-up visit 1 month later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old previously healthy boy was referred for evaluation of a multicystic right hepatic lobe mass and 4 weeks of persistent mild abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four weeks prior to referral, the patient developed fatigue following a fishing tournament, followed the next day by abdominal pain and fever (38.9 C). At a local hospital, he was diagnosed with pneumonia based on chest X-ray findings (with abdominal pain attributed to referred pain) and completed a course of oral antibiotics. Because mild abdominal pain persisted after antibiotic completion, outpatient abdominal CT and MRI were performed, revealing a multicystic right hepatic lobe mass initially suspected to be focal Caroli syndrome, prompting tertiary referral.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for initial fatigue and fever (38.9 C, resolved) and persistent mild abdominal pain (4 weeks).

objective.physical_examination: Fever of 38.9 C documented at initial local hospital presentation.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial local chest X-ray was interpreted as pneumonia. Pre-referral laboratory panel: normal liver function tests (ALT 21 U/L, AST 26 U/L, GGT 10 U/L), normal coagulation (PT 11.6 sec, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 435 mg/dL), mildly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 5.4, ESR 30), normal alpha-fetoprotein (AFP 0.8 IU/mL), and negative serologic antibodies for Entamoeba histolytica and Echinococcus.
objective.advanced_workup: Outside abdominal CT showed a multicystic lesion in the inferior right hepatic lobe; outside abdominal MRI showed serpiginous tubular structures in segment 5 initially interpreted as possible focal Caroli syndrome. Institutional MRI re-review demonstrated clusters of multiple T2-bright circumscribed cystic lesions (<2 cm each) in hepatic segment 6 suggestive of mesenchymal hamartoma. The patient underwent surgical hepatic lobectomy to resect the ~6 x 12 cm mass.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Histopathological examination of the resected ~6 x 12 cm hepatic lobectomy specimen (H&E, 200x) demonstrated puzzle-shaped islands of hepatic parenchyma embedded within a loose hyalinized mesenchymal matrix, confirming a benign hepatic mesenchymal hamartoma (with amoebic liver abscess, hydatid cyst, and hepatoblastoma ruled out by negative Entamoeba histolytica/Echinococcus serologies, normal AFP, and histology). Following complete surgical resection via hepatic lobectomy, the patient had an uneventful postoperative recovery and remained completely asymptomatic at 1-month follow-up.
